brief.situation: 11:00 in an outpatient orthopedic clinic (direct access). You are the physical therapist. Ms. Ferreira, 38, has right neck pain and an occipital headache that began suddenly during a neck adjustment two days ago. She wants 'it cracked back into place'.
handover: She describes the headache as 'unlike any I've had'. This morning she had a spell of double vision and felt unsteady.
Clinic policy: neck pain with headache and any neurologic or posterior circulation sign goes to the emergency department the same visit; no manipulation.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Each check takes the time on its button. Decide what the findings mean, what to stop or start, and who must know.
Partway through you are asked to write your reasoning. A debrief scores what you did.

scoring.modelReasoning: Neck pain and/or headache is the hallmark of cervical artery dissection, often after trauma, and neck manipulation is associated with it. Posterior circulation signs (diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia, dystaxia, nystagmus) raise the concern, and dissection is a common cause of stroke in younger adults. Do not manipulate or provoke; send her the same visit for emergency CT and CT angiography of the head and neck.
